issues: 96 is the count for Book II alone. Book II, 'Intelligence Activities and the Rights of Americans', numbers its recommendations 1 to 96, and Recommendation 96, on Senate oversight, is the last. Book I of the same final report ('Foreign and Military Intelligence', S. Rep. 94-755) has another 87 numbered recommendations, ending with '87. Federal Register for Classified Executive Orders'. So the Senate Historical Office's line 'The final report included 96 recommendations' understates the total. The phrase it quotes, 'to place intelligence activities within the constitutional scheme for controlling government power', comes from Book II's foreword ('Our recommendations are designed to place intelligence activities within the constitutional scheme for controlling government power'). The label and unit are narrowed to Book II.

The notes repeat a unit error from the Senate page. The committee's own reports count pages, not documents: Book II has 'Approximately 110,000 document pages were obtained' and Book I has 'documentation in excess of 110,000 pages'. '40 subcommittee hearings' is also the Senate page's wording; Book II says 'over 40 subcommittee meetings devoted to drafting the two volumes of our final report'. The notes are rewritten on the primary wording.

Date detail, no field change: the Senate page gives 29 April 1976 as the issue date. The printed Books I and II are dated 'APRIL 26 (legislative day, APRIL 14), 1976'. The record gives only the year 1976, which is correct.

issues: Wrong unit. The committee's own final report counts pages, not documents. Book II: 'Approximately 110,000 document pages were obtained from the various intelligence agencies (still more were preliminarily reviewed at the agencies), as well as from the White House, presidential libraries, and other sources.' Book I: 'documentation in excess of 110,000 pages'. The Senate Historical Office's '110,000 documents' is a paraphrase that changes the unit. 110,000 documents would be many times more material than 110,000 pages.
'Reviewed' is also imprecise. The report says the pages were 'obtained', and that more material was only 'preliminarily reviewed at the agencies'.

The value (110,000), year (1976) and '800 witnesses' are correct. Book II: 'Some 800 witnesses were examined, approximately 250 under oath in executive sessions, 50 in public sessions, and the balance in interviews.'

issues: The parenthesis 'the Privacy Act (1974, which binds federal agencies only)' overstates. Section 552a governs federal agencies' records. But section 7 of the enacted Privacy Act (Pub. L. 93-579, uncodified) also binds state and local agencies: 'It shall be unlawful for any Federal, State or local government agency to deny to any individual any right, benefit, or privilege provided by law because of such individual's refusal to disclose his social security account number.' Reworded so it is accurate and still makes the point that the Act does not cover companies.
'no single, comprehensive data protection law covering companies' should say federal. Several US states now have comprehensive consumer-privacy statutes. The absence is at the national level.

fieldFixes.correction: The US has no single, comprehensive federal data protection law covering companies, but Congress passed a string of sector-by-sector statutes in this period: the Fair Credit Reporting Act (1970), the Privacy Act (1974, which governs records held by federal agencies, not companies), the Electronic Communications Privacy Act (1986), and the Computer Matching and Privacy Protection Act and Video Privacy Protection Act (both 1988). The gap is breadth, not existence.
